name: review-flight-deck
title: A reviewer surface above several pull requests
outcome: On every pull request change, the flightdeck simulates several ways to merge the open set, replays the best one or two with real git, and shows the reviewer one validated recommendation told as a story. The alternatives and the reason each lost are one level down.
done_when: A pull request event starts the mode without a person naming a set.
A pull request with no description gets one from /pr:generate before the flightdeck reads it.
The set the reviewer sees excludes whatever the team's own auto-merge rules already handled.
The mode simulates at least three routes from the records, then replays the best one or two with real git and counts the conflicts.
The front page shows one recommendation, written as what would happen rather than as a structure.
The alternatives are visible on the front page and reachable only from inside the recommendation.
Each alternative states the reason it lost, and a git-replayed reason where one exists.
The recommendation names what the replay could not check.
The reviewer acts on a wave from the page, and each action appends one ledger line.
The reviewer opens any pull request in the existing four-level layout, and returns.
The viewer renders the routes and computes none of them.
abort_if: The stop count for a set is not materially lower than the total number of authored files the pull requests change. Measured over 27 pairs of merged pull requests in this bundle, the ratio runs from 0.00 to 0.41, and every pair reduces. This criterion is met for the whole corpus.

Superseded criterion, kept for the record: the first version of this test compared the stop count against the shared-file list, not against the total changed files. That was the wrong baseline, because a reviewer's alternative is reading both diffs in full, not reading the shared subset. On that wrong baseline only 9 of 27 pairs reduce, and pull requests 11 and 12 give 37 stops against 22 shared files.
A proposed partition anchors reviewers more than it helps them, measured against a set they also reviewed without one.

min_work.derived_from: 3 districts touched (viewer, scripts, .cobuilder-architect). 4 colliding ADRs: ADR-0001 (one self-contained file under a blocking content policy), ADR-0018 (one lifecycle surface and a derived record index), ADR-0019 (the append-only ledger, with its vocabulary fixed at comment, reply, and state), ADR-0020 (viewer parts and an author-time build, decided and not executed). 1 boundary rule crossed: no plugin names another plugin's path, so the viewer reaches the proposal through the bundle.
min_work.note: Stage 3 issued six isolated exploration frames and one separate critic pass. Stage 4 raised three challenges and the engineer answered all three. The engineer overruled the recommended approach and chose the Braid and the Cut together, on the ground that both do work on the reviewer's behalf before the reviewer arrives. That choice replaced the stated approach and moved the whole computation terminal-side, which also removed the ledger write-path defect the first challenge raised. Stage 7 asked whether this is one pull request or several. The engineer chose one, so every epic carries the same branch, design/review-flight-deck, and the six epics are units of work inside one review rather than six pull requests. A scratchpad run of E1's arithmetic over the cached diffs corrected the first abort criterion, which compared stops against shared files rather than against total changed files. Round 2: the engineer revised the intent. The mode is named flightdeck. It runs on a pull request event, not on a named set, and it offers several proposals rather than one partition. Each proposal carries a narrative and a diagram. The six epics collapse into four. ADR-0022's boundary holds unchanged. Automatic triggering collides with the no-hooks install rule and is the one open decision. Round 3: the engineer resolved the trigger themselves, with a scheduled skill run or a workflow, and it stops being an open question. The remaining work is the layout and the proposal quality. flightdeck-prototype.html is the layout, close to working: three views, the actions a reviewer takes from the page, a drill-in to the existing four-level layout, and an append-only ledger. Round 4: the engineer set the presentation rules. Show one recommendation, not three. Keep the alternatives visible and unreachable until the reviewer opens the recommendation. Write the story of what would happen, not the structure of the options. Work at the scale of every open pull request, and drop whatever the team's auto-merge already handled. The pipeline becomes simulate from records, then a git what-if on the top one or two, then a validated recommendation. Precomputing mergeable git slices may exist elsewhere, and the narrative plus the options is the part that does not.

epics.outcome: A pull request with no description gets one from /pr:generate before the flightdeck reads it. A pull request that already has one is left alone.
epics.note: New in round 4. It closes the gap the prototype had to show as a warning: 8 of 12 pull requests in this repository carry no intent block. Reuses generate mode whole, and adds only the check for an existing description.

epics.outcome: The mode lists every open pull request with its head branch, changed files, and design, and marks the ones the team's auto-merge rules already handled.
epics.note: The same work as the first epic of the inflight-record-store design. Build it once, in shared code. The auto-merge split is read from the team's own rules, and this design does not define them.

epics.outcome: The mode simulates at least three merge routes for the open set from goal.json, epics, boundary rules, districts, and authored intent. Each route names an order and the evidence for it.
epics.note: divergent-exploration.md already generates competing options in isolation and criticises them in a separate pass. This is that pattern applied to merge orders.

epics.outcome: The mode replays the best one or two simulated routes on a scratch worktree, counts the real conflicts, and promotes the survivor to a validated recommendation.
epics.note: New in round 4, and the step that makes the recommendation something to stand behind. Read-only against a scratch worktree. A route that fails the replay is kept, with the failure as its reason for losing. Systems that precompute mergeable slices may already do this part, so keep the interface narrow enough to swap one in.

epics.outcome: Each route carries a story of what would happen if it were chosen, not a description of its structure. A losing route carries the reason it lost.
epics.note: story-mode covers the register. The worked example the engineer gave: perform the renames and restructuring across the repository, which merges without conflict, then incorporate the new viewer into the resulting structure and naming conventions.

epics.outcome: The front page shows one recommendation and an unreachable marker for the alternatives. Opening the recommendation unlocks them. The reviewer acts on a wave from the page, and each action appends one ledger line.
epics.note: Reuses the existing view modes, the level rail, and the ledger from ADR-0019. flightdeck-prototype.html is the reference layout.
